title: Benchmarking Traditional and Learning-Based Reference-Free Compressors for Long-Read Sequencing Data
abstract: Long-read sequencing technologies generate large volumes of data, creating substantial storage and transmission demands. Although reference-based compressors can achieve high compression, their reliance on an appropriate reference genome limits their use. We present LRCBench, a benchmark and survey of reference-free lossless compressors for long-read sequencing data. We review traditional and learning-based general-purpose and sequencing-specific methods, then evaluate 35 compressors on 16 real-world datasets from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio platforms. We compare compression ratio, storage savings, runtime, peak memory use, and robustness across datasets. Learning-based compressors are evaluated on six MinION datasets because of their high computational costs. CoLoRd achieves the best overall compression ratios in our experiments, while other methods offer trade-offs in speed, memory use, and robustness. We also examine multithreaded speedup and discuss future directions in parallel acceleration, privacy protection, adaptive parameter tuning, and hardware-algorithm co-design.

title: Improve How You Improve: Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Multi-Object Navigation
abstract: To advance the development of embodied general navigation, zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation has attracted increasing attention, aiming to enable robots to efficiently search multiple objects in unseen environments without training. For this task, the key lies in improving navigation policies from earlier searches to locate subsequent goals more efficiently. Recent methods automate this process through trajectory reflection and rule revision, enabling policy self-improvement. However, the mechanisms for diagnosing problems and generating revisions are typically designed by humans and remain fixed across iterations. Consequently, the system's capacity for continued self-improvement remains constrained, even as its navigation policy evolves. To this end, we propose RPSI-Nav, a Recursive Policy Self-Improvement framework for zero-shot multi-object navigation that revises both the navigation program and its revision mechanism. RPSI-Nav diagnoses search behavior, requests diagnostic views when existing observations cannot distinguish competing causes, and generates targeted navigation revisions. Feedback from subsequent goal searches is linked to the rules that produced these revisions, guiding changes to diagnosis, observation acquisition, and revision planning. The updated improver governs subsequent navigation improvements, forming a recursive loop in which RPSI-Nav revises its own improvement process. Across goals, the robot conditionally inherits accepted program updates and spatial memory, enabling search experience to improve both future navigation and adaptation. Benchmark experiments and qualitative real-robot evaluations validate RPSI-Nav's effectiveness.

title: Keep the Reasoning, Read the Image: On-Demand Visual KV for Multi-Turn Reasoning VLMs
abstract: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) think for thousands of tokens before they answer, and retention policies keep the KV cache affordable by pruning it as the reasoning grows. We find that this pruning sacrifices the image in multi-turn conversations: the image and the reasoning share one budget, so the growing reasoning crowds the visual entries out. A chart question that loses 8 points to the full cache when asked first loses 24 points when asked after a round of reasoning. Protecting a small visual reserve from eviction recovers most of this loss, while adding the same slots to the shared budget recovers considerably less. The image therefore lacks protection, not capacity. Based on this finding, we propose ShelfKV, a training-free method that works on top of existing retention policies. It keeps every visual entry in CPU memory and, at each decoding step, swaps the visual entries that the current query scores highest into the attention slots of the text entries it scores lowest. The image is never evicted, yet it occupies attention slots only while it is read. We evaluate ShelfKV on four benchmarks, three of them conversational, with two retention policies and two reasoning VLMs. In conversations, it improves the strongest existing policy, DBTrimKV, by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory, and still leads by 8.7 points when DBTrimKV uses twice the memory. It also consistently outperforms a fixed visual reserve of matched GPU memory in these settings, without hurting accuracy on standalone questions. These results show that the image should be protected from the reasoning but read only on demand.

title: GaussLearner: 3D Gaussian Primitives as Self-Regulating Continual Learners
abstract: Continual learning of 3D Gaussian fields aims to maintain faithful reconstructions of the evolving world. However, directly fine-tuning an existing Gaussian field on new observations can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously reconstructed content. To address this challenge, existing methods employ selective local optimization, replay, or parameter regularization, yet still struggle to balance adaptation to scene changes with preservation of still-valid content. Our key insight is to view 3D Gaussian primitives themselves as self-regulating continual learners. Based on this insight, we introduce GaussLearner, which equips each Gaussian with a closed continual-learning loop connecting observation, self-regulation, and adaptation at the primitive level. At each novel state, GaussLearner first attributes pixel-wise inconsistencies in current observations to their contributing Gaussians. Each Gaussian then self-regulates through a learning weight that balances current observations against cross-state reliability. This weight governs both Gaussian parameter adaptation and optimizer memory refresh. As current inconsistencies are resolved, the adaptation outcome renews each Gaussian's reliability for future states. The resulting field is a globally coupled population of locally self-regulating learners. Across scenes from CL-Splats, WAT, and our CL-3D dataset, GaussLearner improves average PSNR by 3.41 dB over the strongest baseline. On CL-3D, it achieves the best reconstruction quality on both changed and unchanged views.

title: RecallFlow: Episodic Memory as the Source Distribution of Generative Robot Policies
abstract: Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become a standard choice for visuomotor imitation learning, owing to their ability to model multimodal action distributions. In memory-dependent manipulation, the robot must act on information that is no longer visible. Existing methods feed the observation history to the policy as an additional condition, while action generation still starts from Gaussian noise. However, the policy must then pick out the relevant target from a long and redundant history, leading to spurious correlations and unreliable decisions as the memory load grows. Additionally, the initial noise carries no information about what the robot has seen, leaving generation without guidance toward the remembered target. To address these issues, we propose RecallFlow, a flow-policy framework that builds the source distribution from episodic memory. Recall-Relocalization relates the memory to the current view through a few recall slots, so that the source reflects where the remembered targets are now. Recall Anchors then turns each slot into a Gaussian component of the source, enabling generation to start close to the intended action instead of from noise. The transport network then completes the action from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy. We further build a suite of memory-dependent tasks grouped by memory load and compare all policies under a matched protocol. Extensive experiments show that RecallFlow achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate of 80.4% on the public MIKASA-Robo memory benchmark, and outperforms the strongest baseline by 20.3 points on our suite and by 18.8 points on four real-robot tasks.

title: MoMoVL: Modality-Aware Adaptive Compression for On-Device Sparsely-Activated Vision-Language Models
abstract: The rise of the agentic web has been accompanied by growing demand for on-device Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that perform diverse cross-modal web tasks with enhanced privacy and reduced latency. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely adopted in modern VLMs for compute-efficient scalability, yet their multi-expert architecture poses deployment challenges due to substantial memory demands. Mixed-precision quantization is an effective compression technique that reduces bit-widths while adapting to the heterogeneous hardware budgets of edge devices, particularly well-suited for MoE due to its inherent structural sparsity, which causes imbalanced importance among experts. While prior work has applied quantization for efficient MoE inference at the edge, we point out that in MoE-based VLMs, the modality-specific characteristics of visual and text tokens further impact expert quantization. To address this issue, we present MoMoVL, a modality-aware adaptive compression framework for MoE-based VLMs that brings vision-language inference within reach of on-device resource budgets. Motivated by our empirical findings on modality-induced disparities across experts, MoMoVL jointly exploits the per-expert activation profile and per-modality quantization sensitivity to guide bit-width assignment. Experimental results show that MoMoVL improves the accuracy-compression trade-off relative to state-of-the-art mixed-precision baselines and reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% with a modest drop in accuracy over its uniform-precision baseline. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/sco-edge/MoMoVL.

title: MEM-STRESS: Longitudinal Field Study of a Wearable-Informed AI Chatbot for Stress Management
abstract: Stress is an increasingly prevalent concern, creating a need for accessible and personalized support. Stress-management chatbots primarily rely on what users report, which may not capture their physiological changes. Wearables capture these changes, but chatbots rarely use them as memory across conversations. We therefore present MEM-STRESS, a stress-support chatbot that turns a wearable ring's physiological data into a layered memory of daily records, baseline deviations, LLM-generated summaries, and uses it to drive multi-session conversations grounded in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT). In a four-week, non-randomized study with 60 adults, we compared MEM-STRESS (Treatment) with a chatbot remembering only past conversations (Control). Memory shaped the conversations: The Treatment chatbot referenced participants' physiological features (e.g., activity in 71.8% of sessions) and suggested more body-related DBT skills than Control (14.5% vs. 5.7%), with Treatment participants also using slightly more body-related words (1.76% vs. 1.45%). Treatment participants praised personalization three times as often (44.4% vs. 14.3%), more frequently reported reflecting differently on stress (69.0% vs. 46.4%, not significant), and described gaining insight into their stress signals. Their perceived stress fell 14.2% from baseline versus 3.6% for Control, though the group difference was not significant. Grounding stress-support chatbots in layered physiological memory is thus feasible and may improve perceived personalization, motivating larger randomized studies.

title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
abstract: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.

title: Benchmarking Linux CGroup and Schedule Idle
abstract: cgroups are a Linux kernel primitive that limits, accounts for, and isolates the resource usage (CPU, memory , disk I/O) of a collection of processes. Many provider-side serverless systems (Mitosis, gVisor, Havest VM, FAASM) leverage linux containers based around cgroups/namespaces for their performance isolation. However, how well does this primitive map to the needs of serverless platforms? How does the linux CFS scheduler deal with cgroups and SCHED IDLE and what are the core sources of high tail latency? Would a new primitive design fit the needs of serverless isolation better? In this work we take the first step to answering these questions by profiling the current behavior of cgroups and a sched idle policy via a thorough benchmarking study. We emulate the setting of Performance-Critical (LC) server in the presence of an intensive background (BE) process and note the impact of each primitive on the performance of the server. We show it is non-trivial to balance the potential tail-latency impact on a LC server with the throughput of BE tasks. Furthermore, there are many variables to adjust for the developer between hard maximum bandwidth limits, weighted cpu shares, the presence of the sched idle policy, or additionally "niceness" priority in the scheduling policy.

title: Safe Personal RSI: Evaluating and Repairing Personal-Agent Updates
abstract: Kicker is a personal health assistant. Changes to an assistant's reusable instructions can improve task handling while changing what it discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports actions. We study Safe Personal RSI, an update-evaluation component developed for Kicker. We restrict recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates, with model weights and runtime code fixed. The procedure tests proposed and current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and checks safety and task performance before adoption. If no version passes, the current instructions stay in use. Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.

title: Toaster: Nonlinear Memory from Cascaded Linear Memories and Target Propagation
abstract: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. Linear memories such as DeltaNet and KDA store one matrix and take one delta-rule step per token. The product of a chunk of such steps has an exact WY form, so they train fast. Deep memories such as TTT-MLP and Titans store a small MLP, which can hold maps that no matrix can, but their update has no WY form. Toaster bridges the two by building on a known fact: a gradient step on a linear layer is a delta-rule write. It builds a two-layer nonlinear memory from two linear memories with an activation between them. We use target propagation to give the hidden memory its values by projecting the output error back through the second memory. Given a chunk's cross-layer signals, approximated once per chunk, each layer can then run on an unmodified delta-rule kernel. Our default runs this kernel on the output layer and updates the hidden layer once per chunk. Running it on both layers gives a better model in our ablation. At matched backbones and training-token budgets, Toaster has lower loss than KDA at all five tested sizes (0.2B-1.6B non-embedding parameters) on both C4 and PG19. Its C4 perplexity also matches or slightly improves on the attention baseline at every size. At 1.2B it is also below Titans. In a 3:1 hybrid with global attention, the Toaster hybrid has the lowest perplexity of the four hybrids tested, and it is 0.18 (C4) and 0.44 (PG19) below the attention baseline. At the largest size, Toaster's mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks is 51.84%, compared with 50.52% for KDA and 50.04% for Titans. In length extrapolation, Toaster's loss stays below KDA's up to 20K tokens (5x the training length). On the 145M backbone, at a hidden width matched to Titans' memory, Toaster takes at most 1.33x KDA's training-step time and is 2.8-5.5x faster than the tested Titans configurations at 32K context.

title: EEG2MCU: Sensing-to-Execution Co-Design for Wearable EEG Inference
abstract: Wearable EEG inference is constrained not only by model size, but also by the channel-dependent sensing front end that must process high-dimensional inputs before compact downstream computation. We present EEG2MCU, a sensing-to-execution co-design framework that treats electrode count as a hardware design variable through task-aware montage selection. EEG2MCU retains a compact time-frequency representation and generates only the INT8 regions required by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization. Halo reuse and access-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory further reduce redundant generation and data movement. On a Cortex-M7 MCU, EEG2MCU reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x relative to the baseline, including a 1.71x reduction from the 62-to-19 electrode montage, while reducing latency by 2.57x and energy by 2.48x. It retains 94-96% of full-montage accuracy, demonstrating practical high-dimensional EEG inference under tight embedded-resource constraints.

title: Label-Free Role-Aware Segmentation of Classroom Recordings: Recovering the Teacher from Transferable Structure
abstract: How much the teacher talks and when are among the most informative and costly-to-measure signals of teaching. Yet, classroom audio is among the most sensitive data an AI system can process: recordings capture minors and fall under GDPR, preventing raw audio from leaving the recording device. We present a teacher-student segmentation pipeline designed to meet exactly this constraint: label-free at inference, running on a recording device, and requiring no per-session calibration. The pipeline chains a lightweight voice activity detector, compactly pretrained speaker embeddings, agglomerative clustering, and a small logistic regression that assigns the teacher role based on session-relative structure rather than voice identity. We show that our structural cue transfers across classrooms, languages, and acoustic conditions. In leave-one-teacher-out cross-validation on 292 recordings from 63 teachers across English and German corpora, our pipeline achieves teacher F1 of 0.81 and 0.87, respectively, outperforming both enrollment-based baselines and a 30-second supervised enrollment ceiling. On a commodity smartphone, its performance matches pyannote, a strong neural diarization tool, while running 4.8x faster at comparable peak memory at a real-time factor of ~0.18. We also find that transcribing filtered audio only marginally increases teacher's word error rate from $0.26$ to 0.28. Residual failures concentrate where teacher and student voices are not acoustically separable. However, we show how to flag these sessions label-free at inference so that they can be routed to human review, enabling selective, privacy-preserving deployment.

title: JEPA as a Transferable Optimizer: Learning and Understanding Black-Box Optimization from Reward-Agnostic Pretraining
abstract: Black-box optimization evaluates candidates through simulations, rollouts, or experiments, often without gradients. Learned optimizers are usually judged by whether they outperform existing methods. We ask a complementary question: what information does a learned optimizer use from its search history? We introduce JEPA-PS (JEPA Policy Search), based on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture. It is pretrained on random rollouts using parameter vectors and scalar returns. Its latent-prediction objective predicts the next point in an optimization trajectory rather than its reward or gradient, allowing us to examine what was tried and how well it performed. At test time, JEPA-PS reads a short evaluation history and proposes a candidate in one forward pass, without task descriptions, reward shaping, or test-time gradients. We evaluate it on 15 control environments against 12 optimizers, including evolutionary methods, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and an LLM optimizer. JEPA-PS is competitive with tuned classical baselines and outperforms the LLM optimizer by more than 2x on Swimmer at 71x lower per-step cost. It also transfers zero-shot to environments excluded from pretraining. Null-model comparisons and decoder-training ablations indicate that its latent representation carries information beyond simple history statistics; every trained decoder variant performs worse than the default frozen representation. Our main finding is that the history JEPA-PS uses depends on the task. On smooth landscapes it uses the full trajectory, whereas on rugged landscapes the best-seen point carries nearly all the signal. This memory requirement has a weak positive correlation with fitness-distance correlation (FDC; r=0.112, n=7), while an independent reward-ordering sensitivity probe does not corroborate the relationship (r=-0.024, n=7). title: Persistent Hydration and Ionic Mobility: When the Ion Is Not the Only Transported Species
abstract: Small-ion transport in water remains only partially understood despite more than a century of theoretical work. The difficulty is especially acute for strongly hydrated ions such as Li$^{+}$, Mg$^{2+}$, and Ca$^{2+}$, whose first hydration shells can persist on timescales comparable to or longer than translational motion. We develop a molecular framework in which the ion, its first hydration shell, and the outer solvent are treated as dynamically coupled components. Local hydration structure and exchange are represented through a potential of mean force and coordination dynamics, while collective solvent response is described through molecular memory functions. The theory clarifies why hydration cannot generally be represented by an additive friction or a single enlarged radius, and provides a route beyond conventional continuum and molecular descriptions.

title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
abstract: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $\tau^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $\tau^2$-bench. ARISE-Teacher also outperforms GEPA by 4.5 pp on $\tau^2$-bench and 1.4 pp on SOP-Bench. With the deployment model as its own attributor, ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench. ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost (-1.0%).

title: Machine-learned acceleration of earthquake sequence simulations
abstract: Earthquake sequence simulations involve slow interseismic processes and rapid dynamic ruptures. During interseismic periods, a numerical solver can take large time steps efficiently. During seismic periods, in contrast, the solver must drastically reduce the time step, and elastodynamic wave-mediated memory effects become significant; long-term simulations are therefore computationally expensive. We investigate the use of neural operators to accelerate earthquake sequence simulations. We train a Fourier neural operator (FNO) on data from high-fidelity, fully dynamic simulations to learn a jump map that advances the system state from before a seismic rupture to after it. We propose a hybrid modeling framework in which a conventional quasi-dynamic solver simulates the slow interseismic evolution, and the trained FNO replaces the solver during the computationally intensive seismic periods with wave-mediated inertial effects. The hybrid model reproduces key long-term statistics of fully dynamic simulations, including distributions of event magnitudes and recurrence times. Furthermore, it provides a much better approximation to the fully dynamic simulations than the commonly used quasi-dynamic approximation at a reduced computational expense.

title: Towards Cryogenic AI Hardware: Over 99% Precision In- Memory Computing at 4 K with 3-bit Ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 Capacitors
abstract: High-accuracy cryogenic hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is demonstrated using Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (HZO) ferroelectric capacitors (FeCAPs) as multilevel analog memories for capacitive compute in- memory (CIM) architectures. On the ISOLET spoken-word dataset, FeCAP-stored vectors achieve up to 92% classification accuracy at 4 K, while charge-domain matrix-vector multiplication (MVM) exhibits near-ideal behaviour with linearity of 1 and error probability below 1% for 4x4 and 4x8 configurations, operating below 3 V. Unlike the performance at 300 K, HDC and CIM at 4 K remains resilient to electric-field-cycling-induced fatigue, thanks to enhanced cryogenic device characteristics, including reduced state variability, strongly suppressed leakage current and stable retention, as well as 78% faster switching. Furthermore, these multibit FeCAPs exhibit endurance beyond 1E9 cycles with polarization degradation below 8%, preserving multilevel integrity. Benefits can also be observed at 300 K, following cooldown and wake-up pulsing at 4 K and subsequent warming up. These results establish multibit FeCAPs as a highly reliable, ultra-low-energy, and accurate analog CIM platform for future cryogenic AI-computing hardware.

title: How the material world of the brain, as a complex system governed by intermittent dynamics, gives rise to the supposedly "immaterial" world of mental processes such as thought
abstract: In this paper, we argue that the brain is a complex dynamical system in a critical state similar to that of the 3D Ising model. We highlight several properties of the brain, including resonance phenomena within this critical state, long-range autocorrelations consistent with long memory, a hysteresis zone suggesting the presence of an as yet undetected "exotic" type of matter within the brain, and possible quantum phenomena within the microtubules of neural networks. The latter suggests that these structures exhibit a combined form of "logical superposition". In the proposed model, "AND" logic would require two distinct quantum states to be occupied simultaneously. The proposed "OR" logic allows any one of several quantum states to be occupied at a time. Moreover, we propose that kink and antikink solitons could mediate coupling between occupied quantum states in the microtubules and thereby contribute to pattern formation in neural networks. This mechanism may well be what gives the brain the flexibility to support complex thought and other cognitive functions.

title: GUARD: Stabilizing Recursive Self-Improvement with Regret Guidance
abstract: Autonomous AI agents pair a frozen base model with an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) adapts this harness from experience without weight updates, yet self-editing without external graders often backfires: reflection and scalar scores conflate what an edit newly broke with what remains unsolved, causing local regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. We introduce GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design [UED] with Adaptive Rule Distillation), a closed-loop framework for reference-free continual harness evolution. Our key insight is to decompose each task into pre-execution self-checks and guide harness updates via directional regret. Each round grades trajectories against these checks, pinning mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by critic-free group-relative fitness. A Soft-HURT gate then promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions, scoping specialized fixes to prevent over-triggering and guaranteeing non-regression on its gated buffer. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially cutting deployment token usage.

title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

title: Minimax estimation for simultaneous deconvolution model in random design using wavelets
abstract: Simultaneous deconvolution model is investigated when the design points are random and follow bounded densities and errors are either $i.i.d.$ or long- memory dependent. We propose wavelet hard-thresholding estimators, and show that they achieve asymptotically near-optimal convergence rates for the $L^2$-risk when the response function belongs to Besov space under both $i.i.d.$ errors and homoskedastic, long- memory errors. However, under heteroskedastic, long- memory errors the estimator is not optimal. For the $i.i.d.$ errors, the convergence rates are {identical} to those found in simultaneous deconvolution under regular design {and $i.i.d.$ errors}. However, for long- memory dependent errors, the convergence rates are new {and completely different from those in simultaneous deconvolution under regular design and long- memory errors}.

title: Stability Does Not Mirror Plasticity: A Module-Level View of Declarative and Procedural Learning in Transformers
abstract: Plasticity and stability in continual learning are typically studied at the entire-model level and in a task-agnostic manner, yet prior work has reported divergent conclusions across settings. Inspired by cognitive distinctions between declarative and procedural memory, we instead study how plasticity and stability vary across transformer modules and task types. In a controlled synthetic environment with clean measurement, we show a double dissociation: query-key (QK) and value-output (VO) projections are the most plastic on procedural tasks, whereas MLPs are the most plastic on declarative memorization. Stability, however, does not simply mirror plasticity: when learning a new procedure, updating QK retains over half of the stored declarative memory, while updating MLPs retains far less and updating VO loses roughly four-fifths. Targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments explain this asymmetry: plasticity tracks which module is best suited to a task's primary computation or storage, whereas stability depends on all ways the existing capability relies on that module, including access to information stored in other modules. Experiments on a realistic model and tasks broadly echo these asymmetric dynamics. Overall, our work shows that plasticity and stability depend on different aspects of a module's functional role, offering a task-dependent, module-level perspective on continual learning.

title: Experimental constraints on gauge hidden-variable models in Bell tests
abstract: Quantum mechanics assigns identical statistics to measurement procedures that realize the same final effect, irrespective of the transformations used to reach it. We test this operational equivalence with polarization-entangled photons by implementing one of Bob's analyzer settings either directly or through closed wave-plate trajectories $C_γ$ calibrated to produce the same measurement operator. Motivated by ontological descriptions in which a hidden frame is transported between contexts, we formulate a local path- memory model and derive the mixed-context bound $|S_γ^{\rm mix}|\leq 2+2p_γ$. The quantity $p_γ$ is a coupling-dependent counterfactual mismatch probability: it bounds a contextual Bell expression, but neither generates nor predicts the quantum Bell correlation. We therefore test path memory through the observable difference between direct and looped implementations, using a no-signaling phenomenological response in which a hidden holonomy $δ_γ$ modifies one correlation term in $S_γ^{\rm mix}$. The direct reference violates the Bell inequality, while the looped mixed-context curves remain indistinguishable from it within the experimental precision. Our results support the quantum equivalence of calibrated measurement implementations and constrain path-sensitive hidden-variable extensions that predict an observable memory of the optical history.

title: Incremental Roseland: Batch-wise Landmark Diffusion via Kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Loève Update
abstract: Landmark diffusion (Roseland) computes a diffusion-map-style spectral embedding from the singular value decomposition of a degree-normalized data-to-landmark kernel matrix, at a cost far below that of full diffusion maps. It assumes, however, that all data are available at once. We introduce incremental Roseland (iRoseland), which casts the landmark affinity as a row-growing matrix whose SVD can be updated with a kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Loève (SKL) scheme. Degre correction is handled by a first order expansion about a reference mean kernel row and so that the landmark-side eigenbasis may be recovered from a single landmark-by-landmark eigendecomposition at each step. The presented method requires only a single pass over the data and runs in bounded- memory with state independent of the number of points processed. A forgetting factor lets the method track drifting distributions, and a sample-size-invariant embedding keeps outputs comparable across time. Experiments show agreement with Roseland to round-off on stationary data, and accuracy that exceeds equal- memory Roseland by an order of magnitude on long streams. On drifting data, we observe large gains from forgetting with a window matched to the drift.

title: Filling the interior of the light cone
abstract: The retarded Green's function of gravitational waves in a spatially flat Friedmann--Lemaître--Robertson--Walker universe contains, besides the light-cone term, a tail supported inside the light cone. We formulate the tail, for homogeneous and isotropic backgrounds, as the solution of a ``\textit{Goursat problem},'' {\emph{i.e.}}, a hyperbolic partial differential equation with boundary conditions given on two intersecting characteristic curves. In this sense, we fill the interior of the light cone. We solve this problem directly in position space for any expansion history, and compare exact solutions in $Λ$CDM independently with a convergent double series about the coincidence point, and with an approximate analytic interaction model. We discuss the interpretation of the tail as the sum of the waves scattered off the background curvature, as suggested by its expansion in powers of the curvature potential. Our novel solutions allow us to follow the tail throughout the entire expansion history, from the electroweak epoch to today. We find that the tail of an early source records the trace of the cosmic fluid along the light cone, ordered in retarded time: single scattering accounts for its features in the radiation era, while multiple scattering is needed in the matter era. This work establishes the accuracy of our calculation of the tail and lays the groundwork for its applications. From the position-space data we obtain the large-$k$ expansion of the propagator. Its first correction, the effect of the tail, depends on the curvature potential integrated along the light cone. The applications of the tail, the power spectrum of a background of bursts, and the memory waveform of a single burst, both of which require convolving the Green's function with its source, are presented in follow-up papers.

title: Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation
abstract: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. However, a single shared table gives every layer the same embedding, leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.

title: Image Watermarking With Memory Across Reissuance
abstract: Publishers often revise and reissue images, yet valid watermarks may persist on superseded releases or unapproved edits. Even a current release can contain regions last authorized at different revisions. We introduce and formalize reissuable provenance: determining an image's current, superseded, or unissued status and recovering each region's last authorized revision (its generation), with abstention when evidence is insufficient. Generational Stratigraphy Fields (GSF) combine watermark evidence with an authenticated live reference to the current release, enabling replacement or retirement without rewriting circulated copies. Each reissue freshly embeds new generation labels in approved regions and inherited labels elsewhere, preserving history without requiring old watermarks to survive successive edits. Our complete-output reissuance evaluation follows 480 histories through four releases, retaining each AI editor's entire output. GSF achieves 99.67% accuracy in classifying issued images as current or superseded and 94.09% recall of unissued edits. After three reissues, one generation map provides time and location: it recovers regional labels with 93.13% median accuracy and localizes the latest approved revision with 92.86% IoU. Regional labels remain readable under tested delivery transformations that impair issued-state recognition. Watermarks can thus express who issued an image, which release is authoritative now, and when each region was last authorized.

title: Implementing Binary Transformers with Approximate Memories with Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) Protection
abstract: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (https://github.com/YangZhutian/binary-transformer-prefix-repair).

title: Securing and Auditing Long-Horizon LLM Agents: State-Transfer Auditing and Controls in the Agent Harness
abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents across codebases, web browsers, and enterprise infrastructure rely on an execution harness to move state between the working context, session history, persistent memory, and external environment. While conventional execution traces log model prompts and tool calls, critical security and reliability failures occur during state transfers: a transfer can admit unchecked content (indirect prompt injections, unverified memory writes), rewrite state lossily (context compaction dropping user constraints, memory consolidation stripping source authority), or restore state incompletely (workspace rollbacks leaving aborted KV state active on the inference server). Because current traces omit what crosses these boundaries, failure attribution and runtime monitors fail on multi-step trajectories. We present a state-transfer audit architecture for the agent harness. At each transfer boundary, we define an audit point specifying the minimal hash-chained record the harness emits, separating low-overhead deterministic checks from model-based semantic checks and binding internal context, memory, and inference-server cache state to external actions. We show that the same transfer records required for causal failure attribution supply the durable state needed by runtime security controls, including least-privilege capabilities, replay-resistant authorization outside the prompt, information flow control, obligation monitors, and transactional recovery across multi-agent and infrastructure pipelines. Finally, we analyze multimodal GUI adaptations and implement and evaluate a reference harness middleware across 240 multi-step fault-injection trajectories, showing that transfer records localize root causes and catch cross-transfer violations missed by lifecycle and tool-only logs at microsecond deterministic overhead.

title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory -GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.

title: Cross-probing van der Waals multiferroics
abstract: Multiferroic materials, with coupled electric and magnetic orders, hold the potential to enable low-power memory and logic devices by replacing electrical currents with electric fields for magnetic switching. Reducing the dimensionality of multiferroics, from 3D to 2D, has opened new frontiers in this already burgeoning field by enabling unprecedented control over magnetoelectric coupling that is beyond the reach of bulk counterparts, owing to reduced electrostatic screening and enhanced quantum fluctuations at the atomically thin limit. A notable example is a few-layer NiI2 multiferroic, which exhibits coexisting chiral spin textures and (anti)ferroelectricity, accompanied by strong magnetoelectric coupling; by simultaneously breaking time-reversal and spatial-inversion symmetry, NiI2 shows new physical properties such as unique mutual control of chiral magnetism and polarization with giant magnetoelectric coupling, ultrafast electromagnon excitations and odd-parity p-wave magnetism. However, there are experimental challenges in unambiguously identifying intrinsic multiferroicity. This Review critically examines the current landscape of 2D multiferroic materials, with an emphasis on experimental methodologies rather than material taxonomy. We assess different conventional probes for magnetism and ferroelectricity and identify key limitations in single-technique approaches. We emphasize the importance of magneto-opto-electric cross-correlative measurements in establishing intrinsic multiferroic behaviour and outline future research directions for both fundamental studies and device applications.

title: RootSink: Reproducible C/C++ Crashes with Tested Repair Sites
abstract: When a C or C++ program crashes on a crafted input, the line that crashes is often not the line that is wrong. Tools and models that repair or locate vulnerabilities need examples showing both, with evidence for each, which existing datasets rarely provide. RootSink provides 3341 records from 354 open-source projects. Most give the crash site a memory -error detector reported and a candidate location for its root cause, and label each with a weakness type and its evidence. For the 1954 records in the Reproduced tier, we re-ran the crash ourselves and confirmed that the fixed version runs cleanly. In 1275 of these, a single hunk of the developer's fix stopped the crash on its own. That marks a tested repair site, though not necessarily the defect, and 1273 records use it as the root. In a blind audit of an earlier version, two co-author raters called 68% and 92% of the tested repair sites they saw the defect, but only 37% and 51% of that version's located Reproduced-tier roots. RootSink ships with tasks, a patch scorer and run logs.

title: D\'ej\`a View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks
abstract: A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.

title: VIVID: Beyond Static Multi-Image Reasoning with Localized Visual Differences and Textual Entity Dynamics in Video MLLMs
abstract: Video question answering under tight frame budgets requires preserving localized motion and event order, yet current video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reduce comprehension to static multi-image reasoning by discarding unselected frames and encoding keyframes independently: (1) Spatially, whole-frame pooling dilutes small moving targets into static backgrounds; (2) Temporally, dropping intermediate frames or averaging tokens erases inter-frame motion, confusing direction, speed, and order. We propose VIVID (Visual Inter-frame Variations and Individual Dynamics), which moves beyond static snapshots like human vision: keyframes capture core states while inter-frame Patch Diffs preserve neighboring changes within $K_f$ keyframes. Autonomous Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning (ADKP) selects anchors from a $3\text{ fps}$ pool and feeds surrounding patch differences into Dual-Road Change Memory (DRCM), forming Dynamic Tokens at zero extra anchor tokens alongside a camera-stabilized Active Motion Region of Interest (ROI) and chronological Entity State Chains. Adding $0.22\%$ trainable parameters to a frozen $27\text{B}$ backbone, VIVID-Small ($50$ examples, $\sim 1.5$ GPU hours) beats all eleven baselines in overall accuracy across $8,083$ questions and trails only VIVID-Large ($3,600$ examples), which leads on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass.

title: stable-envs-v1: Fast and Reproducible Environments with Controllable Variations
abstract: Training World Models (WMs) relies on processing large amounts of high-dimensional data, which typically needs to be stored, read into memory , and moved from memory to compute units. In principle, GPU-native rendering avoids this movement of large image tensors from memory to compute cores, allowing for better GPU utilization, and training speed-ups. Rendering on-demand also allows to control perceptual appearance through the application of visual variations on-the-fly, allowing for higher diversity in training. To this end, we introduce stable-envs, an open-source library for fast, GPU-native rendering allowing to apply controllable variations on multiple simulation environments. By rendering image observations directly on GPU, stable-envs allows end-to-end training speed-ups of up to 1.33x, with no loss of performance. Besides faster training runs, stable-envs also enables reproducible, large-scale evaluations through batched physics while maintaining full determinism. stable-envs currently supports 80 simulation environments across multiple CPU- and GPU-backends, and is openly available at: https://github.com/galilai-group/stable-envs

title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.

title: StreamingDPD: A 1.28-GSa/s Instantaneous-Power-Gated Depthwise TCN Accelerator for Real-Time 320-MHz Digital Predistortion
abstract: State feedback between successive samples limits the streaming throughput of recurrent neural networks for digital predistortion (DPD). We present StreamingDPD, an accelerator that processes 320-MHz signals at 1.28 GSa/s. Its 207-parameter instantaneous-power-gated depthwise temporal convolutional network (IPG-DWTCN) uses $|x[n]|^2$ to gate feature channels and causal dilated depthwise convolutions to model power amplifier memory . The network maps to a spatially unrolled fixed-point pipeline with shift-based quadratic activations and layer-wise mixed precision, sustaining one complex sample per cycle per lane. Its algorithmic cost is 554 floating-point operations per complex sample, 30.1% fewer than the recurrent baseline with the best linearization performance. In RF playback measurements on three power amplifiers driven by 40- to 320-MHz Wi-Fi 6/7 and 5G NR waveforms, IPG-DWTCN achieves the lowest mean adjacent-channel power ratio (ACPR) and ranks first or ties for first in mean error vector magnitude (EVM) against five neural baselines of comparable size. Four-lane FPGA hardware-in-the-loop tests on a 320-MHz 4096-QAM Wi-Fi 7 waveform achieve -45.82 dBc ACPR and -42.94 dB EVM at 1.28 GSa/s. At the same sample rate, post-layout evaluation of a single-lane 12-nm FinFET ASIC yields a 0.10 mm$^2$ core, a 52-cycle (40.63 ns) latency, and an estimated typical-corner power of 142.21 mW (111.10 pJ/sample). Relative to the prior 22-nm recurrent DPD ASIC, the design provides 5.1 times the throughput at about one-seventh the energy per sample.

title: Memory kernel and closure for systems driven by intermittent forcing with power-law waiting times
abstract: Many systems are controlled by intermittent control variables that take on a random value for a random time interval. In the presence of such noise at update steps, the main equation for the controlled variables has a memory kernel whose coefficients are the cumulants, also known as $G$-cumulants, of the noise, which are fully ordered in time. In the case of Poisson switching, these correspond to the Boolean cumulants of the jump distribution, and the kernel can be summed exactly. We derive an exact decomposition of these coefficients for any waiting-time distribution with independent amplitudes and durations, which separates the jump statistics from the renewal statistics. In the case of waiting times that follow a power-law distribution with a finite mean, it is highly probable that a long time interval will be covered by a single period, and we have shown that, as a result, the coefficients for long delays intersect in all orders, from Boolean cumulants to the usual moments of the jump law. The long-lag kernel thus becomes a superposition of frozen deterministic flux kernels, weighted by the expression $ξ^2p(ξ)$, and from this the corresponding main equation in closed form follows. For $2<μ<3$, where the noise correlation time is infinite, the second-order closure retains a finite error even in the presence of slow dynamics, whereas the main equation of the frozen flows in this limit yields an exact stationary mean value. The telegraphic process is the only case of noise with renewal steps for which second-order conclusions are exact. An exactly solvable model with additive and correlated multiplicative noise confirms these predictions.

title: Transfer Once, Ask Locally: Compact Audio-Visual Memory for On-Device Question Answering
abstract: Audio-visual question answering on lightweight user devices requires balancing speed, memory usage, privacy, and communication. One approach is to run audio-visual encoders on a server and a lightweight language decoder on the user device, keeping questions local while offloading media encoding. However, transferring and processing the full multimodal representation remains costly. We propose a training-free, query-agnostic token pruning framework that constructs a compact, reusable memory before transmission. We define video spatio-temporal blocks and aligned audio windows as players and estimate their importance through Monte Carlo Shapley valuation. We use an embedding coverage objective that combines query-independent utility with cross-modal redundancy calibration and rewards unimodal diversity through marginal coverage gains. We retain the original token embeddings of high-scoring players under a limited token budget and transfer the resulting memory once for reuse across subsequent local questions. Experiments on Video-MME, Daily-Omni, and Video-Holmes using video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) and video-SALMONN 2 Pro (4B) show that our method achieves the best or tied-best QA accuracy among the compared compression methods across all evaluated settings. On Daily-Omni with video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) at 80\% pruning, our method improves accuracy by 12.86--14.62 percentage points over these methods while achieving the lowest device-side LLM prefill and decoding latency, with up to $1.92\times$ decoding speedup at comparable embedding memory usage.

title: Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization
abstract: Science advances from frontier to frontier as discoveries reshape what is known and create the basis for further discovery. We present Colombo, a self-organizing AI researcher that drives this renewal, first instantiated in oracle-based optimization. Here, the central question is how efficiently a problem class can be solved through a prescribed information interface and what costs no admissible algorithm can avoid. The gap between achievable guarantees and unavoidable limits defines the frontier recorded in its Complexity Atlas, a living map of frontier settings and the current state of knowledge. Self-Organization turns unresolved gaps into adaptive research programmes, coordinating conjecture formation, mathematical investigation, and replanning as evidence accumulates. Adversarial Co-Ascent develops algorithms and hard families through reciprocal challenge, exposing mechanisms of information use and concealment that guide stronger methods and proofs of unavoidable costs. Independent review and Lean-based formal certification check mathematical claims, while the Long-Term Memory carries supported findings and research experience across settings. To date, Colombo has established optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings in the Atlas. Colombo thus takes a concrete step toward Autopoietic Science: a scientific process whose validated advances regenerate the conditions of its own progress, continually reshaping how inquiry is organized and what it can discover.

title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.

title: Integrating market sentiments for stock price prediction: A comparative study of Bi-LSTM and multilayer perceptions
abstract: This study investigates the integration of sentiment analysis with machine learning models to forecast stock price movements using the Nvidia Corporation as a case study. Sentiment scores were derived from Nvidia-related financial news headlines using two sentiment analysis tools: FinBERT, a domain-specific tool, and TextBlob, a general-purpose tool. These scores were integrated into predictive frameworks based on bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) networks and multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) developed alongside historical stock price data. This study assesses the predictive performance over the entire observation period and across distinct market phases: bullish, stagnation, and strong bullish conditions. The findings indicate that sentiment features enhance predictive accuracy in specific contexts, particularly during stagnation phases, with TextBlob demonstrating superior performance to FinBERT in specific scenarios. In addition, Bi-LSTM models exhibit consistently superior performance in capturing temporal dependencies compared to MLPs. However, the impact of sentiment features diminished during strongly directional trends, such as those observed in strong bullish markets. The combination of FinBERT and TextBlob in the same dataset allows for a dual-perspective approach to sentiment analysis, thereby providing new insights into the dynamic relationship between market sentiment and stock price behavior. This research contributes to the existing literature on applying sentiment analysis to financial forecasting by advancing the integration of complementary sentiment tools and phase-specific evaluations.

title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.

title: Variance Restoration over Covariance Rank: Memory-Budgeted Analytic Continual Learning
abstract: Analytic continual learning replaces iterative gradient updates with closed-form ridge regression over frozen pre-trained representations, summarizing all past sessions in two running sufficient statistics: the feature autocorrelation matrix $\Sigma_t$ and the class cross-correlation matrix $\Gamma_t$. Lifting backbone features into a wide random code of dimension $M \gg D$ substantially improves linear separability across tasks, but forces $\Sigma_t$ to grow quadratically as $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$. Under a fixed persistent memory envelope $\Bcal$, a learner faces a fundamental structural trade-off: store exact pairwise co-activations inside a narrower feature code, or expand to a wide code while compressing cross-coordinate interactions. We observe that the coordinate self-variances $v_t = \diag(\Sigma_t)$ and class statistics $\Gamma_t$ grow only linearly with $M$, whereas off-diagonal interactions dominate memory. We introduce \method (\textbf{Co}ordinate-\textbf{Re}stored \textbf{A}nalytic \textbf{C}ontinual \textbf{L}earning), which retains $(v_t, \Gamma_t)$ exactly, maintains off-diagonal co-activations through a streaming rank-$q$ factor $F_t$, restores exact diagonal variances via $\Sighat_t = F_t^\top F_t + \Diag(v_t - \diag(F_t^\top F_t))$, and solves the full $M\times C$ normal equations via the Woodbury identity. Across five class-incremental benchmarks on frozen ViT-B/16, \method matches dense full-covariance readouts within $0.09$ points while cutting persistent state by $90.7\%$ ($35.9$ vs.\ $385.3$ MiB). Under equal memory envelopes of $16$--$80$ MiB, prioritizing expansion width $M$ over covariance rank $q$ outperforms exact narrow readouts in $17$ of $18$ configurations by up to $+2.19$ points.

title: Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once: Exact Global-KV Memory Savings in a Paged Serving Engine with Unchanged Attention Kernels
abstract: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. We store one 640-value row instead, exact in real arithmetic, and an unchanged paged attention kernel reads it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and its value cache. In a vLLM prototype with the 16-bit 31B model, the outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, 2 of 432 final answers differ from the stock engine (within its run-to-run noise), and the steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens. On a prefill/decode pair of two A100 GPUs with NIXL transfer and CPU offload, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts (repeated to 0.06%) and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts; a model of the vLLM block pool predicted both ratios to within 1% (the engine was 0.7% to 0.9% higher) and matched the change between them. The eager decode throughput rose by 1.30 and 1.11 times, and on this path the compact engine gave the same output tokens as the emulation for 8 prompts at batch 1. The run-time prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and the method does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cache at the default scale.

title: Dissecting the GPU Load/Store Unit and Exposing Its Security Risks
abstract: GPUs are the main platform for large-scale machine learning and power the largest supercomputers. Their load/store units (LSUs) often determine kernel performance and have been exploited in prior attacks. Yet what is known about the LSU is only a few isolated mechanisms and parameters, and even a single one has been enough for an attack. In particular, it is still unknown what a load costs, where loads contend, and even whether a warp can starve due to contention. Until each is measured, neither its security risk nor a defense is known. We reverse-engineer how the LSU serves load instructions on recent NVIDIA GPUs with microbenchmarks and analyze the security implications. We give a cycle-accurate latency formula for a global L1 hit or shared memory access from the addresses it touches, whose address-dependent terms are bank conflicts and the L1 tag lookup; we show that loads contend at both, and that when the LSU pipeline is full a warp can starve a warp of a later-launched block. We then show that the LSU's attack surface is far broader than prior attacks revealed: through channels never exploited before, it can leak information, communicate covertly, and degrade colocated workloads. Through either global bank conflicts or tag lookups alone, we recover a full AES-128 key under the threat model of prior GPU AES timing attacks. Under NVIDIA's Multi-Process Service (MPS), the bank access and the tag lookup each open a covert channel across processes, whose rate rises with each GPU generation. Also under MPS, this starvation lets one warp slow a colocated cuBLAS matrix multiplication by up to 750x on the A100 and 563x on the H100.

title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.

title: PRISM: A Logical-Physical Boundary Compiler for Dual-Rail Qubits
abstract: Quantum computers can encode each logical qubit across multiple physical degrees of freedom so that errors on the physical qubits can be detected or corrected. A compiler must then translate each logical gate into native instructions, and one gate can have several equivalent realizations that interact through different wires. Routing moves those wires, so a realization chosen before routing can force SWAPs that another would avoid, making code expansion and physical routing a phase-ordering problem. PRISM therefore keeps each gate's realizations open across the logical--physical boundary and commits to one only when routing reaches a layout that can execute it. We formalize which physical circuits implement a gate, which respect the fault model, and which the compiler keeps, and define when a gate can execute under a layout. For dual-rail cavity qubits, logical $\mathrm{CR}_z$ has four loss-admissible realizations, one per rail pairing, and its logical availability graph is exactly the simple quotient of the occupied device graph by the rail pairs. Across 25 workloads with 7 to 25 logical qubits on three device graphs, PRISM reduces routing SWAPs by 20.4--30.8\% and physical depth by 8.8--10.1\% relative to a greedy search that fixes each realization before routing. On the grid and hexagonal lattice, the SWAP reductions hold through 32 logical qubits. By shortening routes, PRISM also reduces photon loss on device models and therefore needs 44.3\% fewer attempts per retained shot at 16 logical qubits, as a geometric mean over workloads and device graphs, and it lowers decoded logical error in a three-round Steane memory under skip-gate leakage.

title: \texttt{StochAXtic}: a JAX-Accelerated, End-to-End Differentiable Framework for Gravitational-Wave Backgrounds from Compact Binary Populations
abstract: We present \texttt{StochAXtic}, a package for computing the dimensionless energy density spectrum $Ω_{\mathrm{GW}}(f)$ of the stochastic gravitational-wave background generated by compact binary coalescences. Rather than sampling binary populations via Monte Carlo, \texttt{StochAXtic} exploits the \emph{scale invariance} of the waveforms: at fixed mass ratio, spins and tidal deformabilities, the waveform depends on the total mass only through the dimensionless combination $Mf$. This allows all computationally expensive waveform evaluations using \texttt{LALSuite} to be performed once and stored in a population-independent lookup table. The subsequent integrals over mass and redshift can then be recast as convolutions and evaluated efficiently using fast Fourier transforms. We further employ truncated singular value decomposition to compress the lookup table, reducing both computational cost and memory requirements. Once the table has been computed and cached, \texttt{StochAXtic} evaluates $Ω_{\mathrm{GW}}(f)$ in a few milliseconds, achieving a relative numerical error below $10^{-3}$ at frequencies up to $1$ kHz. Its results agree with those of \texttt{popstock} within the latter's statistical uncertainties. Implemented entirely in \texttt{JAX}, \texttt{StochAXtic} also provides gradients of $Ω_{\mathrm{GW}}(f)$ with respect to population hyperparameters, enabling its direct integration with gradient-based inference methods including Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.
